sections.h2: Where is the Franklin County Recorder, and what does it record?
sections.html:
The Franklin County Recorder is on the 18th floor of the Franklin County Courthouse, 373 South High Street, Columbus. The phone is (614) 525-3930, and questions can go to recorder@franklincountyohio.gov. The office records, preserves and retrieves real estate, personal property and other records so property interests are safeguarded and easy to find.

The Auditor and the Recorder are different offices in this county. The Auditor handles ownership changes and fees for the transfer, while the Recorder files the deed itself. Mixing up the two is the most common reason a deed gets sent back.

sections.h2: What is the order of steps to record a deed in Franklin County?
sections.html:
File with the Auditor first, then the deed reaches the Recorder. The Recorder's own guide spells out the sequence:

  • Prepare a new deed form. A template is available through the County Law Library under real estate forms.
  • Get the legal description from the last deed on file, which the Recorder's website lets you search, and follow the county document standards.
  • Sign the deed in front of a notary.
  • File the deed with the Auditor and pay the Auditor's transfer charges.
  • Include a separate payment for the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards the deed to the Recorder once the transfer is complete.

Paying off a mortgage does not call for a new deed. The lender files a release of mortgage as its own document.

sections.h2: What does recording cost at the Franklin County Recorder?
sections.html:
The Recorder bases its fees on Ohio Revised Code 317.32 and publishes a fee calculator for checking your math. The table gives the rates as the Recorder prints them.

ItemFee
First two pages$34
Each additional page$8
Document that fails standardization requirements$20
Each indexed marginal reference$4
Debit or credit card payment3% convenience fee
No self-addressed stamped envelope supplied$1 document return fee

Source: Franklin County Recorder fee page. Make checks and money orders payable to the Franklin County Recorder, since checks payable to second or third parties are refused. Cards are limited to Discover, Mastercard and Visa. The statute shows where the $34 and $8 figures come from: each is a base fee plus a housing trust fund fee of the same amount.

sections.h2: What does the Franklin County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?
sections.html:
The Auditor's transfer and conveyance office handles more than 30,000 property transfers a year. Its fee calculator describes a conveyance fee of $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, made up of $1 per $1,000 set by the State of Ohio and $2 per $1,000 set by the Board of Commissioners. There is also a $3 minimum and a $0.50 transfer tax on any transfer that is not exempt. An exempt transfer owes only the $0.50.

When the seller is receiving the homestead exemption at the time of transfer, the county's $2 piece is waived and the conveyance fee drops to $1 per $1,000. You can verify homestead status on the Auditor's property search under the Homestead Credit entry on the parcel summary. Round the sale amount up to the next $100 when you use the calculator.

  • Pay by cash, business check or cashier's check made out to the Franklin County Auditor.
  • Personal checks are not accepted, and the office can give change only on cash.
  • Do not add payments for other county offices to the same check.
  • Transfers must carry the exact amount to be processed.

Questions go to the Transfer and Conveyance Department at 614-525-3253.

sections.h2: Can I e-record a Franklin County deed?
sections.html:
Yes, but only through Simplifile, and mostly for professionals. The Recorder does not run an e-recording platform itself. Private companies, including CSC Global, ePN, Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile, send documents in for recording and may add their own charges.

Deeds that transfer real property can be e-recorded through the Auditor, Engineer and Recorder, though only via Simplifile, and they need to come from a title company, bank or similar entity. Individuals may e-record other documents through Simplifile, but an individual's e-recording cannot transfer property. If e-recording is out of reach, mail the deed or bring it to the 18th floor.

The Recorder also accepts documents completed with electronic and online notarization that meet Ohio legislature and Secretary of State requirements.

sections.h2: Who gets the original deed back, and can I redact my address?
sections.html:
The original returns by mail if you enclose a self-addressed, stamped envelope. Without one, the Recorder charges postage or the $1 return fee on its fee page.

Regular filers can open an escrow account at the Recorder with a starting deposit of $100 or more, so they do not bring a check for each filing. Certain public servants whose home addresses are exempt from public record may ask to have the address redacted from documents posted on the Recorder's website, using the Request to Redact Address form and emailing it to the Recorder.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Franklin County itself?
sections.html:
Franklin County was created April 30, 1803, less than two months after Ohio became a state, and was named for Benjamin Franklin. It covers about 544 square miles and had 1,323,807 residents in 2020, which makes it the most populous county in Ohio. Columbus is the county seat and the state capital.

The county touches Delaware, Fairfield, Licking, Madison, Pickaway and Union counties. Interstates 70, 71 and 270 cross it, along with U.S. 23, 33, 40 and 62. Suburbs on the county list include Bexley, Dublin, Gahanna, Grandview Heights, Grove City, Hilliard, New Albany, Upper Arlington, Westerville and Worthington. Ohio State University's main campus, with about 60,000 students, sits in Columbus.

All of these places record deeds at the same courthouse, so a house in Dublin and a house in Whitehall follow the same path through the Auditor and then the Recorder.

faqs.q: How much does the Franklin County Recorder charge for a deed?
faqs.a: The Recorder lists $34 for the first two pages and $8 for each additional page. A $20 fee applies if the document misses the standardization requirements, and cards carry a 3% convenience fee.

faqs.q: Do I file with the Auditor or the Recorder first in Franklin County?
faqs.a: The Auditor first. After the transfer is complete, the deed goes to the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards it if you included a separate payment for the Recorder.

faqs.q: Does a deed need a notary in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder's guide says all transfers must be signed in front of a notary, and electronic or online notarization is accepted when it meets Ohio requirements.

faqs.q: What is the Franklin County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The Auditor's calculator lists $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, with a $3 minimum and a $0.50 transfer tax. The fee drops to $1 per $1,000 if the seller receives the homestead exemption.

faqs.q: Can an individual e-record a deed in Franklin County?
faqs.a: An individual can use Simplifile for some documents, but an individual's e-recording cannot transfer property. Deeds that transfer property come through a title company, bank or similar entity.
